1.pericope_label: In the three and twentieth year of Joash the son of Ahaziah king of Judah Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned seventeen years. And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, and followed the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, which made Israel to sin; he departed not therefrom. And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he delivered them into the hand of Hazael king of Syria, and into the hand of Ben–hadad the son of Hazael, all their days. And Jehoahaz besought the Lord, and the Lord hearkened unto him: for he saw the oppression of Israel, because the king of Syria oppressed them. (And the Lord gave Israel a saviour, so that they went out from under the hand of the Syrians: and the children of Israel dwelt in their tents, as beforetime. Nevertheless they departed not from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, who made Israel sin, but walked therein: and there remained the grove also in Samaria.) Neither did he leave of the people to Jehoahaz but fifty horsemen, and ten chariots, and ten thousand footmen; for the king of Syria had destroyed them, and had made them like the dust by threshing. Now the rest of the acts of Jehoahaz, and all that he did, and his might, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? And Jehoahaz slept with his fathers; and they buried him in Samaria: and Joash his son reigned in his stead.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the verb for beseeching literally as stroking the face of the Lord, insists the hearkening was not immediate since the Syrian invasions were renewed throughout the reign, makes the saviour the grandson rather than the son, reads the Asherah as the sacred tree of Assyrian art sacred to Ashtoreth, takes the subject of the clause about the fifty horsemen to be the Lord himself, and reads the small remnant of cavalry as evidence of complete disarmament.

Gill rules out four candidates for the saviour before settling on Joash, guards the prayer by denying it was heard for the king's sake or for a repentance that was only external, reads the intervening verses as a parenthesis, and makes the king of Syria the one who left Israel only fifty horsemen.

Clarke opens with the regnal arithmetic, that Jehoahaz began at the commencement of the twenty-third year of Joash and reigned seventeen years, fourteen alone and three alongside his son; he identifies the saviour as Joash undoubtedly, reports Houbigant's recommendation that the verses be read in another order, and names the goddess of the grove under both her names. Wesley fixes the blame for the grove on Ahab who planted it and on the failure to destroy it as the law required, and draws the inference that Israel was not conquered through any cowardice in its king but by the righteous judgment of God.

debates: Who the promised saviour was: not an angel nor a captain nor Elisha nor Jehoahaz but his son Joash (Gill), Joash undoubtedly (Clarke), or the grandson Jeroboam, of whom the next chapter says the Lord saved Israel by his hand (Ellicott).
How the broken sequence of verses 4 to 7 is to be read: as a parenthesis resumed at the fifty horsemen, which Gill and Ellicott agree on, or simply in another order, as Clarke reports from Houbigant.
Who it is that had left Jehoahaz only fifty horsemen, where Gill makes it the king of Syria and Ellicott the Lord.
outliers: Ellicott observes that the verdict on the northern worship is written from the standpoint of an editor living long after the events, and that it does not appear from the histories of Elijah and Elisha incorporated in his work that either prophet ever protested against the worship established at Bethel and Dan.
Wesley reads the note on the king's might as deliberate, inserted to show that the defeat was not the fault of his courage.

10.pericope_label: In the thirty and seventh year of Joash king of Judah began Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz to reign over Israel in Samaria, and reigned sixteen years. And he did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord; he departed not from all the sins of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel sin: but he walked therein. And the rest of the acts of Joash, and all that he did, and his might wherewith he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel? And Joash slept with his fathers; and Jeroboam sat upon his throne: and Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel. Now Elisha was fallen sick of his sickness whereof he died. And Joash the king of Israel came down unto him, and wept over his face, and said, O my father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof. And Elisha said unto him, Take bow and arrows. And he took unto him bow and arrows. And he said to the king of Israel, Put thine hand upon the bow. And he put his hand upon it: and Elisha put his hands upon the king’s hands. And he said, Open the window eastward. And he opened it. Then Elisha said, Shoot. And he shot. And he said, The arrow of the Lord’s deliverance, and the arrow of deliverance from Syria: for thou shalt smite the Syrians in Aphek, till thou have consumed them. And he said, Take the arrows. And he took them. And he said unto the king of Israel, Smite upon the ground. And he smote thrice, and stayed. And the man of God was wroth with him, and said, Thou shouldest have smitten five or six times; then hadst thou smitten Syria till thou hadst consumed it: whereas now thou shalt smite Syria but thrice.

schools.summary: Ellicott declines to harmonise the date and accepts the Greek reading thirty-ninth as simply right; he attends to how a bow is held and reads the prophet's hands over the king's as investing the act with a prophetic character, renders the saying as an arrow of victory for the Lord and over Aram, limits the prediction to the army at Aphek rather than the forces of Syria, and sets the whole scene in the ancient practice of soothsaying by arrows, analogous in principle to casting lots.

Gill harmonises the regnal date by supposing either imperfect years or a two or three year co-regency, so that Jehoahaz lived to see his prayer answered; he states plainly that the prophets do not live for ever and that Elisha died rather than being translated, raises a geographical objection to the eastward window since Syria lay northeast or more north, and reads the number of strokes as a measure the prophet left to the king's own will so as to learn his spirit.

Clarke harmonises the same way on Calmet's authority, dates the illness to the tenth year of Joash and reckons sixty-five years of prophesying, takes the window as facing the country beyond Jordan that Hazael had seized, supplies at length the ancient custom of shooting an arrow or casting a spear into a land about to be invaded, and adds the guard that Elisha's anger at three strokes does not prove that God was wroth or had intended more; Wesley reckons sixty years from the prophet's first call.

debates: How the thirty-seventh year is to be reconciled with the earlier notice: by imperfect years or a co-regency (Gill, Clarke with Calmet), or by emending the figure to thirty-ninth on Greek manuscript authority (Ellicott).

Which way the eastward window faced, where Clarke takes it as the trans-Jordan country Hazael had seized while Gill objects that Syria lay northeast or more north, so that the eastward part of Israel may be meant.

What the three strokes signify and why the prophet was angry, where Ellicott reads a divination whose result the prophet left to the king's impulse, Gill a measure of the spirit in which he would pursue his victories, and Clarke warns that the prophet's anger proves nothing about God's intention.
outliers: Clarke notes that the king's cry over the dying prophet is the very cry Elisha himself had raised at Elijah's translation.
Ellicott adds the qualification that it is not implied the prophet's hands were still on the king's when the arrow flew.

20.pericope_label: And Elisha died, and they buried him. And the bands of the Moabites invaded the land at the coming in of the year. And it came to pass, as they were burying a man, that, behold, they spied a band of men; and they cast the man into the sepulchre of Elisha: and when the man was let down, and touched the bones of Elisha, he revived, and stood up on his feet. But Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz. And the Lord was gracious unto them, and had compassion on them, and had respect unto them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them, neither cast he them from his presence as yet. So Hazael king of Syria died; and Ben–hadad his son reigned in his stead. And Jehoash the son of Jehoahaz took again out of the hand of Ben–hadad the son of Hazael the cities, which he had taken out of the hand of Jehoahaz his father by war. Three times did Joash beat him, and recovered the cities of Israel.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the raiders as troops who used to invade and supposes a lost preposition in the note of time, backs Houbigant's conjecture on the word order of the raising, reports Thenius on the miracle as a pledge of Elisha's promise, takes the verse about grace for a remark of the compiler written when the northern kingdom had already perished, notes that the successor is absent from the Assyrian records and that his name was a divine title, and argues that the recovered cities must have lain west of Jordan.

Gill lays out the authorities on where Elisha was buried and how long he prophesied without adjudicating between them, and ends by preferring Kimchi, that he died at the beginning of Joash's reign while the son was still partner in the throne; he explains the successor as the third of that name, retained because it was respectable with the Syrians, and places the recovered cities in Gilead and Bashan.

Clarke compares the two prophets and ventures that it is hard to tell whether Elijah was a man or an angel in a human body, answering the obvious objection that being fed by an angel proves nothing since God manifest in the flesh was fed by the same ministry; he reconstructs the hurried burial, concludes that the prophet worked no miracle by his own power but by God's, and turns the episode against the whole system of miraculous working relics; on the verse about grace he works its three verbs devotionally.

debates: Where Elisha was buried and how long he prophesied, where Gill reports Epiphanius for a city of Samaria against the Jewish tradition of the cave on Carmel, and sixty, sixty-six or a death at the beginning of Joash's reign.

How the clause about the raising is to be construed, where Ellicott backs Houbigant in reading that the party departed and then that the man touched the bones, against the rendering that the man went and touched them.
Where the recovered cities lay, Gill placing them in Gilead and Bashan and Ellicott arguing they must have been west of Jordan since the trans-Jordan had been subdued in the time of Jehu.
outliers: Clarke makes the raising the first and, he believes, the last true miracle performed by the bones of a dead man, and observes that on it and the like the whole system of miraculous working relics has been built.

Ellicott reads the verse about God being gracious as the compiler's own remark, on the evidence of its style, its appeal to the covenant, and the phrase as yet, which he takes to mean until the day he was writing.
